name: Salmon
lede: Salmon is the orange-pink of the fish's flesh, and on screens it is a bright, warm pink that sits between coral and peach.

sections.title: The name and its family
sections.body:
Paterson defines salmon as the orange-pink of the fish's flesh, and notes that Salmon, capitalised, is one of the 140 colours of the X11 set, with the code #FA8072 [1]. He also lists salmon pink as a deep pink and salmon red as an orangey-red [1]. St Clair's glossary calls it a warm pinky orange [2].

The family on our side is wider than those entries: [[salmon-pink]], [[dark-salmon]], [[light-salmon]] and [[flesh-color]] all lean on the same word, and [[coral]], [[peach]] and [[flesh-color]] sit close to it. The books do not say when the word first became a color name.

sections.title: Where the color turns up
sections.body: St Clair notes that the women painted by the rococo artists Boucher and Fragonard are dressed in salmon-coloured silks [3]. Finlay met young weavers in a village who found salmon-pink in rock lichens that they call *muzgo de roca*, one colour in a wild-collected set that ran to deep browns from walnuts and blacks from mimosa [4]. In gems, the pink beryl found in Madagascar in 1911 was named [[gem:morganite|morganite]] in gratitude to the financier J. P. Morgan, and Finlay says it usually comes out of the ground a pale salmon and looks far more vivid after heating [5].

sections.title: Dead Salmon, and other Salmons
sections.body: The British paint firm Farrow & Ball sells a colour called Dead Salmon that is so off-white it is almost brown, and it is a best seller [6]. The name has nothing to do with the fish dying: it comes from an invoice for decorating a house in 1850, where it meant a dead flat finish [6]. Finlay reports that the National Trust objected to the name [6].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The screen color is #FA8072, a lightness of 67 and chroma of 54, and ISCC-NBS 1955 calls the nearest block vivid yellowish pink, 4.8 units away [7]. Other sources do not agree on what salmon is: Ridgway's 1912 swatch is the duller #E49489, and the xkcd survey of 2010 chose the redder #FF6163 [7].

Birren, writing in 1950, recommended tints of orange such as peach and salmon for hospitals, homes, factories and schools, which is an old opinion and not modern evidence [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Bright salmon is almost absent from oil painting. Only one of 23,781 paintings in our archive carries a color within six ΔE units of it over at least five per cent of the canvas, the 1860 [[painting:commons-Q133269393|Self-portrait]] by Emma Gaggiotti Richards, at 16 per cent [9]. A wider lens finds it in nine paintings, 0.04 per cent, rarer than 77 per cent of the named colors [9].

In printed English the word itself peaks in the 1880s, though the count includes the fish [10]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [9].
